problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14059356/assets/db924dbe346c279e307d0b75b29cbccbfab566c251f90e3a63024264d5a512e5.png)

Consider the RC circuit shown above. Given that the charge $q(t)$ of the capacitor at time $t$ seconds is given by

$$
q(t)=A{e}^{-4t}+\frac{P}{425}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\frac{Q}{425}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)
$$

where $A,$ $P,$ and $Q$ are constants, find the value of $P+Q.$

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*
worked_solution:
The diagram shows a series RC circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $12\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor with resistance $100\,Ω,$ and a capacitor of capacitance $0.0025\,\text{F}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs. 

$$
I=\frac{\text{d}q}{\text{d}t}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RC circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=100\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=100I=100\,\frac{dq}{dt}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{0.0025}=400q.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
12\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)=100\,\frac{dq}{dt}+400q,
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{dq}{dt}+4q=\frac{3}{25}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t).
$$

This is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. So, to find the general solution, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${q}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{d{q}_{c}}{dt}+4{q}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{q}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-4t},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal with argument $t,$ i.e.,

$$
{q}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{p} & =\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(t), \\ \frac{d{q}_{p}}{dt} & =-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(t)+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(t)+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(t))+4(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(t)) & =\frac{3}{25}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) \\ (-\alpha +4\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)+(4\alpha +\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) & =\frac{3}{25}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}-\alpha +4\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)) \\ 4\alpha +\beta =\frac{3}{25}\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =\frac{12}{425},\beta =\frac{3}{425}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{q}_{p}(t)=\frac{12}{425}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\frac{3}{425}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
q(t)={q}_{c}(t)+{q}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-4t}+\frac{12}{425}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\frac{3}{425}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t).
$$

Therefore, we have $P=12,Q=3,$ and

$$
P+Q=12+3=15.
$$

The current I, measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge q, measured in coulombs. I=dqdt

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RC circuit, there are two voltage drops:

  • The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality R=100Ω. So, VR=100I=100dqdt.

  • The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by q=CVC. Therefore, VC=q0.0025=400q.

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge q on the capacitor is 12cos⁡(t)=100dqdt+400q, which gives dqdt+4q=325cos⁡(t).

This is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. So, to find the general solution, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

  • To find the complementary solution qc, we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by dqcdt+4qc=0. Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution qc(t)=Ae−4t, where A is a constant of integration.

  • Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument t. So, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal with argument t, i.e., qp(t)=αcos⁡(t)+βsin⁡(t). To find the values of α and β, we substitute qp=αcos⁡(t)+βsin⁡(t),dqpdt=−αsin⁡(t)+βcos⁡(t), into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side: (−αsin⁡(t)+βcos⁡(t))+4(αcos⁡(t)+βsin⁡(t))=325cos⁡(t)(−α+4β)sin⁡(t)+(4α+β)cos⁡(t)=325cos⁡(t) Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations: {−α+4β=0(equating the coefficients ofsin⁡(t))4α+β=325(equating the coefficients ofcos⁡(t)) Solving this system gives α=12425,β=3425. Therefore, the particular solution is qp(t)=12425cos⁡(t)+3425sin⁡(t).

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

q(t)=qc(t)+qp(t)=Ae−4t+12425cos⁡(t)+3425sin⁡(t).

Therefore, we have P=12,Q=3, and P+Q=12+3=15.
